1191.title: The Fire That Wept Silver
1191.hook: the gods' treasure, a fire that won't give it back, and tears that turn to silver: why sacred stories sit beside the rules
1191.carry: arthavada: the sacred stories praise what dharma asks
1191.tomorrow: a boy comes home after twelve years of study. what didn't he learn?
1191.howItsDone: In a Satyanarayan puja, families pause the worship to hear the katha, short stories that praise the vow and its prasad, then finish with arati and share the prasad; Mimamsa readers call a story that praises the act beside it arthavada.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mimamsa called the Veda apaurusheya: words with no author, and a bond of word and meaning nobody invented.
screen: `NO AUTHOR.` · `NOW: THE STORY BESIDE THE RULE.`

segments.voice: The gods are about to go to war with the asuras, and they need somewhere safe for their treasure. So they leave it with Agni, the fire. Bad choice. Agni decides he likes it, and he runs off with it. The gods chase him down and take it back by force. And Agni weeps. His tears fall, and they turn into silver. That's a story from the Yajur Veda, in the Taittiriya Samhita. And it ends with a rule: so don't give silver as the gift on the sacred grass at the sacrifice, or within a year there'll be weeping in that house.
screen: `THE GODS' TREASURE.` → `AGNI RUNS OFF WITH IT.` → `HIS TEARS TURN TO SILVER.`

segments.voice: Mimamsa had a problem with stories like that one. For Jaimini, the Veda is about dharma, what is to be done. But a fire weeping silver doesn't tell anyone to do anything. So Jaimini lets an objector speak: passages that ask for nothing have no purpose. Shabara, his great commentator, points to exactly this line, the one where the god wept. Jaimini's answer became a rule of reading. These passages are called arthavada, and they belong together with the command beside them. The story is there to praise or warn about the act. Nobody is meant to take away a fact about where silver comes from. They're meant to feel why the rule matters. Here's the teaching, plainly. In Hindu practice, the story and the duty travel together. The story is how dharma gets into the heart. You can see it in homes today. At a Satyanarayan puja, the family stops in the middle of the worship and listens to the katha, short stories of a poor man, a woodcutter, a merchant who kept postponing his promised puja, a king who walked past the prasad some cowherds offered him. Many teachers read those stories the way Mimamsa reads the Veda: they praise the vow and the prasad, so the act lands. So when a story is told beside a ritual, Mimamsa says, listen for the act it's praising. That's our last day with Mimamsa.
screen: `A STORY THAT ASKS FOR NOTHING?` · `ARTHAVADA: IT PRAISES THE ACT.` · `STORY AND DUTY TRAVEL TOGETHER.` · `THE KATHA AT THE PUJA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing your family does at home, a lamp, a prayer before food, touching an elder's feet, and the story you were told about it, if there was one. Hold the act and the story side by side for a few breaths, and ask what the story was praising. If you pray, you can offer that act once more, slowly, today. If no story comes, just do one small act with care and let that be enough.
Mimamsa. The school that reads the Veda as what is to be done, where even the stories, arthavada, are there to praise the act that's asked for.
screen: `MIMAMSA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: arthavada, the sacred stories praise what dharma asks. Listen for the act inside the story. Until tomorrow.

1192.title: Shvetaketu Comes Home
1192.hook: a son comes home after twelve years of study, sure he knows it all, and his father asks one question he can't answer
1192.carry: after the doing comes the wish to know brahman
1192.tomorrow: Bhrigu asks his father what Brahman is. why won't his father just say?
1192.howItsDone: Students of Vedanta traditionally begin the Brahma Sutra with its first line, the wish to know Brahman, read through their lineage's commentary, often Shankara's, Ramanuja's or Madhva's, and the Chandogya's story of Shvetaketu is one of the best-known ways the Upanishads are taught.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Mimamsa: arthavada, the fire that wept silver, and stories that praise the act being asked for.
screen: `MIMAMSA: STORY AND DUTY TOGETHER.` · `NOW, VEDANTA.`

segments.voice: In the Chandogya Upanishad, a boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Veda. At twenty-four he comes back. He's learned all of it, the hymns, the rites, and he walks in, as the text puts it, full of himself, sure he's learned. His father, Uddalaka, lets him settle. Then he asks one question. Did you ask your teachers for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `HOME, FULL OF HIMSELF.` → `ONE QUESTION HE CAN'T ANSWER.`

segments.voice: So Uddalaka shows him. Know one lump of clay, and you know everything made of clay. The pot and the bowl are just names, shapes, words. What's real is the clay. Shvetaketu is stunned. My teachers can't have known this, he says, or they'd have told me. Please, you tell me. And the father begins the teaching we'll hear more of this week: underneath everything there is one reality, which the Upanishads call Brahman. That's Vedanta, the Veda's end, the teaching of the Upanishads. Its root text, the Brahma Sutra, opens with one short line: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. The great commentators stop on its first word. Now, after what? Shankara says: after a person learns to tell the lasting from the passing, cools toward rewards, gathers calm, and longs to be free. Ramanuja says: after the study of ritual, the earlier inquiry. Two readings, kept side by side. Either way, the teaching is plain. In Hinduism, doing the rites well is not the end of the road. A day comes when a person who has kept the fasts and lit the lamps asks what all of it rests on. That wish is honored, not suspected. It's where Vedanta begins. Shvetaketu didn't lose his twelve years. He finally asked what they were for.
screen: `KNOW THE CLAY, KNOW EVERY POT.` · `ONE REALITY: BRAHMAN.` · `NOW, AFTER WHAT? TWO READINGS.` · `THE RITES AREN'T THE END.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you do out of habit or faith, a prayer, a fast, a lamp, a way you greet your elders, and do it in your mind, step by step. Then let one quiet question rise: what does this rest on? Don't answer it. Hold the wish to know, the way Shvetaketu finally did. If you pray, you can ask it in the presence of the One you pray to.
Vedanta. The Veda's end, the teaching of the Upanishads, which opens with the wish to know Brahman, the one reality under everything. Today's word.
screen: `VEDANTA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: after the doing comes the wish to know Brahman. Like Shvetaketu, ask what it all rests on. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1193.title: Bhrigu Asks His Father
1193.hook: a son asks his father to teach him Brahman, and the father only points: go find where everything comes from
1193.carry: brahman: where everything comes from, lives in, returns to
1193.tomorrow: salt disappears in a cup of water. where did it go?
1193.howItsDone: In traditional Vedanta study, teachers explain the Brahma Sutra's second line alongside Taittiriya Upanishad 3.1 and 2.1, and the Bhriguvalli, Bhrigu's climb from food to bliss, is chanted and taught as part of the Taittiriya.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vedanta began with Shvetaketu: after the doing comes the wish to know Brahman.
screen: `THE WISH TO KNOW.` · `THEN WHAT IS BRAHMAN?`

segments.voice: In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a young man named Bhrigu goes to his father, the god Varuna, and asks straight out: sir, teach me Brahman. And his father won't hand him an answer. He gives him a few things to look at, food, breath, sight, hearing, mind, speech, and then one pointer. That from which these beings are born, by which they live, and into which they go when they leave: seek to know that. That is Brahman. Then he sends his son off to find it himself.
screen: `TEACH ME BRAHMAN.` → `NO ANSWER, ONE POINTER.` → `GO FIND IT.`

segments.voice: So Bhrigu sits with it, in tapas, deep, disciplined attention. He comes back: Brahman is food. Everything is born from food and lives on it. His father doesn't argue. He just says: seek it again, through tapas. Keep looking. Bhrigu goes deeper. Brahman is breath. Keep looking. Brahman is mind. Keep looking. Brahman is understanding. Keep looking. And the last time, Bhrigu understands: Brahman is bliss, ananda. From bliss these beings are born, by bliss they live, into bliss they return. That's the big teaching. Brahman isn't someone up in the sky, apart from the world, and it isn't one thing in the world. It's what the whole world comes from, rests in, and goes back to. The Brahma Sutra's second line says almost exactly Varuna's words: Brahman is that from which the birth and so on of this world come. Even schools that worship Brahman as a loving, personal God, like Ramanuja's, say the whole world lives within him. Vedanta teachers explain it with a picture: a parent shows a child the thin new moon by pointing at a branch just below it. The branch isn't the moon. It gets the eyes there. The Upanishad gives another line too, Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite, and some readers, Shankara among them, hear even that as pointing. And notice how Bhrigu learned. Each answer was true, and not the last word. Many teachers read his climb, food, breath, mind, understanding, bliss, as a path inward any seeker can walk.
screen: `FOOD. BREATH. MIND. UNDERSTANDING.` · `BLISS: ANANDA.` · `NOT A THING: THE SOURCE OF THINGS.` · `A BRANCH POINTING AT THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Climb Bhrigu's steps slowly. Feel your body, fed by food. Then your breath, coming and going. Then your mind, busy or quiet. Then the knowing that notices all of it. Then rest past the knowing, in whatever peace is there, without naming it. If you pray, you can let that peace be your prayer to the One you love.
Vedanta. Today, how it points to Brahman: that from which the world is born, by which it lives, into which it returns, and, Bhrigu found, bliss. Today's word.

1194.title: Salt in the Water
1194.hook: a father drops salt into water overnight and tells his son, "you are that", and three great teachers hear it three ways
1194.carry: tat tvam asi: three great readings, none ranked
1194.tomorrow: a dead teacher's hand has three fingers folded. what did he leave undone?
1194.howItsDone: Hindus in the Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita lines each study the Upanishads through their own teacher's commentary, Shankara's, Ramanuja's or Madhva's, and the line tat tvam asi is read and taught in each lineage in its own way.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vedanta, Bhrigu climbed from food to bliss: Brahman, where everything comes from, lives in, and returns to.
screen: `BRAHMAN: THE SOURCE.` · `AND YOU?`

segments.voice: Back to Shvetaketu and his father. Uddalaka hands him a lump of salt. Put this in a cup of water, he says, and bring it to me in the morning. Next morning: give me the salt. Shvetaketu looks. It's gone. Taste the water from the top. Salty. From the middle. Salty. From the bottom. Salty. You can't see it, his father says, but it's there, all through. That finest essence is the self of all this. That is the real. That is the self. You are that, Shvetaketu. In Sanskrit, tat tvam asi.
screen: `SALT IN THE WATER OVERNIGHT.` → `GONE, YET SALTY EVERYWHERE.` → `TAT TVAM ASI. YOU ARE THAT.`

segments.voice: Tat tvam asi is one of the most loved lines in Hinduism, and here's the teaching inside it: your atman, your deepest self, is not cut off from Brahman. But how? Three of Vedanta's great teachers honor this same line and hear it differently. Shankara reads it straight. You, at your deepest, are Brahman, not part of it. Advaita teachers use the space inside a clay pot: break the pot, and the space was never separate. His school is Advaita, not-two. Ramanuja keeps the self real. In another Upanishad, the sage Yajnavalkya speaks of the one who dwells within all things, whose body they are, who guides them from inside. So for Ramanuja, the world and every self are like Brahman's body: truly real, never apart. You are that, the way a body belongs to the one who lives in it. His school is Vishishtadvaita. Madhva hears difference. For him, the Lord, whom he knows as Vishnu, and the self are always two, and the self depends on him completely, like a reflection that's real only because something shines. His school is Dvaita, two. Three readings, each argued from the same words, and Hindus in each line live and pray by them today. None is ranked here. What all three share is the salt: the self is never on its own, outside the sacred.
screen: `ATMAN AND BRAHMAN.` · `SHANKARA: NEVER TWO.` · `RAMANUJA: THE WORLD AS GOD'S BODY.` · `MADHVA: ALWAYS TWO, ALWAYS CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Let the words come quietly, you are that. Hear them first as Shankara might, as open space no pot ever divided. Then as Ramanuja might, held from inside, the way a body belongs to the one who lives in it. Then as Madhva might, noticing you didn't make yourself shine. A few breaths each. You don't have to choose. If you pray, you can let the line rest in the name you pray to.
Vedanta. Today, the line you are that, heard as not-two, as body and soul, and as two who stay close. Today's word.
screen: `VEDANTA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: tat tvam asi, three great readings, none ranked. Like salt in water, the self is never outside the sacred. Same time tomorrow.

1195.title: Ramanuja's Promise
1195.hook: a young man arrives too late to meet his teacher, finds three fingers folded on the dead man's hand, and makes three promises
1195.carry: every vedanta school writes on the same shared books
1195.tomorrow: Indra keeps going back to his teacher for 101 years. what is he looking for?
1195.howItsDone: In Vedanta lineages, students read the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahma Sutra through their own school's commentaries; Sri Vaishnavas honor Ramanuja's Shri Bhashya, and tell how he vowed to write it at Yamuna's side.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vedanta, salt in the water: tat tvam asi, you are that, heard three ways and ranked by none.
screen: `ONE LINE, THREE READINGS.` · `ONE SHARED SHELF.`

segments.voice: Here's a story Sri Vaishnavas tell about Ramanuja. Yamuna, the great teacher at Srirangam, is dying, and he's heard of a brilliant young man and sent for him. Ramanuja hurries to Srirangam. He's too late. Yamuna has died, and three fingers of his right hand are folded down. People say the teacher left three wishes unfulfilled. So Ramanuja makes three vows out loud, and one of them is to write a commentary on the Brahma Sutra. As he speaks, the story says, the fingers open.
screen: `TOO LATE TO MEET HIS TEACHER.` → `THREE FINGERS FOLDED.` → `THREE VOWS. THE FINGERS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Why would a dying teacher care so much about a commentary? Because of how Vedanta works, and it's a real teaching about Hinduism. Vedanta schools don't start new scriptures. They stand on a shared shelf that tradition calls the prasthanas, the starting points. The Upanishads, what was heard, shruti. The Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna in the Mahabharata, a text of what was remembered, smriti. And the Brahma Sutra, the short, packed lines that gather what the Upanishads teach and answer objections. Shankara wrote on the Brahma Sutra and the Gita. Ramanuja kept his vow and wrote his Shri Bhashya on the Brahma Sutra, and on the Gita too. Madhva did the same. That's how a school stands up: by showing its reading fits the shared texts, all of them, hard verses included. The Brahma Sutra says why early on. Brahman is known from the Upanishads because they all fit together around it. The texts aren't a pile; they're meant to agree. So here's what that means today. Hindus from different traditions, a Shiva temple, a Vishnu temple, an Advaita study circle, a Krishna temple, may describe God differently, and many still revere the same Upanishads and the same Gita. The Vedanta schools' arguments are arguments about how the same pages fit. Nobody wins by changing the subject.
screen: `THE STARTING POINTS.` · `HEARD, REMEMBERED, REASONED.` · `EVERY SCHOOL WRITES ON THE SAME SHELF.` · `DIFFERENT TEMPLES, SAME GITA.`

segments.voice: Let one line you love come to mind, a verse from the Gita, a bhajan, something an elder told you, and say it inwardly, slowly. Ask what's here you haven't seen before. Don't hunt for a clever answer. Stay, the way a commentator stays with a single line, and see what it shows you. If you pray, you can hold that line as an offering.
Vedanta. Today, its shared shelf: the Upanishads, the Gita, the Brahma Sutra, and every school showing how they fit. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: every Vedanta school writes on the same shared books. Different readings, one shelf. Until tomorrow.

1196.title: Indra Stays 101 Years
1196.hook: a god and a demon go to learn the self; the demon leaves happy with the wrong answer, and Indra keeps coming back
1196.carry: moksha: freedom from the round of birth and death
1196.tomorrow: Arjuna asks to see Krishna as he really is. why does he need new eyes?
1196.howItsDone: Hindus speak of moksha, release from samsara, as life's highest aim, and many elders pray for it; traditional students read the Brahma Sutra from its first line to its last, 'no return', said twice, usually through their own lineage's commentary.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramanuja's promise: every Vedanta school writes on the same shared books.
screen: `THE SHARED SHELF.` · `THE LAST LINE.`

segments.voice: Near the end of the Chandogya Upanishad, Prajapati, the creator, announces: there is a self free from old age, death, grief, hunger and thirst. Whoever finds it gains everything. The gods send Indra. The asuras send their king, Virochana. They live as students for thirty-two years. Then Prajapati tells them: look at yourselves in a pan of water, dressed in your best. That's the self. Virochana goes home delighted. The body is the self! And that's what he teaches. Indra gets halfway home and stops. Wait. If the body grows old and dies, that can't be it.
screen: `A SELF BEYOND DEATH AND GRIEF.` → `VIROCHANA: IT'S THE BODY!` → `INDRA: WAIT.`

segments.voice: So Indra goes back. Thirty-two more years. Prajapati says: the self is the one who roams in dreams. Indra thinks it over: but in dreams you can still suffer. Back again, thirty-two more years. The self is the one in deep sleep. But then you know nothing at all. Back once more, five more years, a hundred and one in all. And Prajapati finally says: this body is mortal, held by death, but it's the home of the self that doesn't die. That's the teaching: atman, the self, isn't the body, and knowing it frees you. Hindus call that freedom moksha, release from samsara, the round of birth, death and rebirth. The Chandogya ends with the one who reaches Brahman: he does not return, he does not return. And the Brahma Sutra, which opened with now, the wish to know, closes the same way: no return, said twice. The schools fill in what freedom is. For Shankara, it's knowing what was always so: the self was never anything but Brahman. For Ramanuja and Madhva, the freed self stays itself and lives with the Lord, whom they know as Vishnu, in a joy that doesn't end. So when an elder says she prays not to come back, she isn't asking for less life. She's asking for freedom. Like Indra, she just wants the real answer.
screen: `DREAM? DEEP SLEEP? KEEP GOING.` · `THE SELF ISN'T THE BODY.` · `NO RETURN, SAID TWICE.` · `SHE'S ASKING FOR FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Sit and notice your body, the weight, the warmth. That's known. Then notice your thoughts passing, like a dream. That's known too. Then ask gently, like Indra: who is knowing all this? Don't answer. Rest in the knowing for a few breaths. If you pray, you can rest in the presence of the One you pray to.
Vedanta. From the first word, now, the wish to know, to the last, no return, said twice: freedom. Today's word, and the last of our visit with it.

segments.voice: Your line: moksha, freedom from the round of birth and death. Like Indra, don't stop at the first answer. Rest well.

1197.title: Arjuna's Divine Eye
1197.word: each as a lens for a week
1197.hook: Arjuna asks to see Krishna as he really is, and Krishna says: not with those eyes. why Hindus go to the temple to see
1197.carry: darshana: to see and be seen; six ways of seeing
1197.tomorrow: a rumor at the bus stop: how would Nyaya check it?
1197.howItsDone: Hindus go to the temple for darshan, standing before the deity to see and be seen, often timed to when the shrine's curtain opens; the six darshanas are traditionally grouped in pairs, Nyaya with Vaisheshika, Samkhya with Yoga, and Mimamsa with Vedanta.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Indra stayed a hundred and one years: moksha, freedom from the round of birth and death, and the Vedanta book that ends no return, twice.
screen: `VEDANTA: NOW TO NO RETURN.` · `NOW: HOW HINDUS SEE.`

segments.voice: On the battlefield in the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna has been listening to his friend and charioteer, Krishna, for chapters. And then he asks for something bold. If you think I can bear it, show me your real form, your whole self. Krishna agrees, with one catch. You can't see me with these eyes of yours. I'll give you a divine eye. And Arjuna sees: the whole universe in one body, without beginning, middle or end, brighter than a thousand suns. He's shaking. Afterward, he begs Krishna to take his gentle, familiar form again.
screen: `SHOW ME YOUR REAL FORM.` → `NOT WITH THOSE EYES.` → `A DIVINE EYE.`

segments.voice: Here's the teaching inside that story: in Hinduism, seeing is itself a sacred act. Hindus don't usually say they go to the temple just to pray. They say they go for darshan, to see the deity, and to be seen by the deity. Standing before the image, eyes open, receiving a glance back: that is worship. Arjuna's story says something more. What you see depends on the eyes you bring. The same word, darshana, names the six classical schools of Hindu thought. Each is a way of seeing. We've walked through all six, and one way to hold them is by the question each keeps asking. Nyaya: how do I know? Vaisheshika: what is this made of? Samkhya: who is watching? Yoga: what is the mind doing? Mimamsa: what is this act for? Vedanta: what does all of it rest on? Those are our short versions, not their own words. Think of the eye doctor clicking lenses in: better like this, or like this? The letters don't change. What comes into focus does. Over the next days we'll try the lenses two at a time on ordinary moments: a rumor, a flash of anger, a sink full of dishes. Not to pick a winner. This part of the path is called schools of thought, never ranked. Like Arjuna, you're just asking for eyes that can see more.
screen: `DARSHAN: TO SEE AND BE SEEN.` · `WHAT YOU SEE DEPENDS ON YOUR EYES.` · `SIX SCHOOLS, SIX QUESTIONS.` · `LENSES, NOT RIVALS.`

segments.voice: If you have a deity's picture or an image at home, sit before it with your eyes open, and simply look, and let yourself be looked at. If not, look at something living, a plant, a face in a photo, the sky. Then ask one of the six questions, softly: what does this rest on? Let it go, and keep looking. If you pray, you can let this looking be your prayer.
Each as a lens for a week. The six darshanas, ways of seeing, held not as rivals but as lenses you can try one at a time. Today's word.
